planting.note: Anchor bare-root cuttings or potted crowns in a submerged pot of heavy garden loam set 6 to 24 inches below the water surface once the water has warmed in spring.

directions: Grow fully submerged in clear, slow-moving or still water as an oxygenating native found in Texas spring runs such as the San Marcos and Comal rivers, where constant-temperature flow keeps it green year-round. The thin, grass-like leaves form loose mats below the surface, and in warm months small six-petaled yellow flowers rise just above the water on thread-like stalks. It spreads readily from stem fragments and rooted nodes, so site it in a contained planter basket if a pond is small, and thin occasionally to keep open water for fish and other plants. Provide full sun to partial shade and avoid letting the water level drop enough to expose the crown.

planting.note: Set rooted divisions or plugs directly into saturated mud at a spring seep, pond margin, or the shallowest shelf of a water feature after the coldest nights have passed.

directions: Give this low, mat-forming relative of the common monkeyflower a saturated, muddy margin along a pond edge or a shallow planting shelf, matching the constant-temperature spring seeps of central Texas where it naturally roots into submerged gravel and silt. Rounded, glossy leaves carpet the ground and send up short stalks of small, bright yellow, two-lipped flowers through most of the warm season wherever moisture is dependable. It spreads by creeping stems that root at each node, quickly knitting together an evergreen edge planting in frost-free winters, though hard freezes will kill it back to the crown. Keep it constantly wet and divide congested clumps every year or two to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Transplant rooted sections into shallow, cool, flowing water over a gravelly or silty bottom, such as a stream-fed pond margin or a submerged planting crate anchored in moving water.

directions: This feathery-leaved member of the carrot family is a hallmark plant of the cool, constant-flow spring runs of the Edwards Aquifer, where it grows rooted in gravel with foliage trailing in the current alongside Texas wild-rice habitat. Divided, celery-scented leaves stay submerged or sprawl at the water surface, and small white flower umbels appear above the waterline in warm months on stems that root wherever they touch wet substrate. It performs best with real water movement and cool temperatures, so a recirculating stream or spring-fed water feature suits it far better than a stagnant tub. Thin congested mats periodically, since it spreads steadily by rooting stem fragments.

planting.note: Press rooted plugs into saturated mud or a shallow submerged pot at a pond margin; it establishes quickly once its creeping stems contact consistently wet soil.

directions: Round, coin-shaped leaves on upright petioles rise in neat rows from creeping, rooting stems, forming a low groundcover for the shallow, saturated margins of a pond or spring-fed bog garden. Tiny greenish-white flowers cluster in distinctive whorled tiers around the upper stem in summer, giving the species its common name, though the bloom is more curious than showy. It tolerates both standing shallow water and simply wet soil, spreading quickly as a living mat that helps stabilize muddy banks and the edges of water features. Trim or lift sections as needed to keep it from crowding out neighboring marginal plants.

planting.note: Anchor rooted winter buds or potted rhizomes in a weighted container of heavy clay-loam set on the pond bottom, 1 to 4 feet deep, once spring water temperatures rise.

directions: Broad, wavy, olive-green leaves float just beneath the surface on long stems rooted in the pond or stream bottom, making this a reliable submerged oxygenator for larger water gardens and fish ponds. It is one of the native pondweeds found in the clear, cool, spring-fed waterways of central Texas, where steady flow and good light keep it vigorous through most of the year. Small greenish flower spikes occasionally poke above the water in summer, but the main value here is the dense underwater growth that shelters fish fry and absorbs excess nutrients. Confine the roots to a planting crate in small ponds, since it spreads readily by rhizome and can otherwise fill a shallow pool.

planting.note: Divide and set clumps into shallow submerged pots or directly into mucky bottom soil at the edge of a pond or spring-fed water feature in spring.

directions: This stout, leafless marginal rush forms upright tufts of round, hollow, dark green stems tipped with small brown seed spikelets, giving a vertical, grassy accent at the shallow edge of a pond or water garden. It grows naturally in the mucky margins of spring-fed wetlands and coastal marshes across the southern United States, tolerating both standing water and saturated soil equally well. Plant it in submerged pots or directly in a boggy margin alongside pickerelweed or arrowhead for a textural contrast of fine vertical stems against broader foliage. It spreads gradually by rhizome and can be divided every few years to control its spread or to start new pots.
